methodology: PRICING METHODOLOGY  |  how these rates are built, how new ones get added, and how to turn them into a budget
SECTION 1  -  HOW THE EXISTING PRICES ARE STRUCTURED
The event production spine - technical, venue, stage, staging, medical, catering, stationery, HR, security, protocol. The large majority of priced lines.
Contracted third-party rates. Fixed and already negotiated.
Use as-is. Do not re-estimate. If a figure looks wrong, query the vendor rather than overwrite it.
Marketing and communications - packages, consultancy, strategy, brand, digital, content. Also IT/Wi-Fi and post-event reporting.
Published agency rate card, largely productised into fixed-scope packages.
Use as-is, but check scope: package prices assume a defined deliverable count, so confirm the inclusions before comparing against a bespoke quote.
Videography and live-streaming variants only (7 lines).
An earlier internal price list retained alongside the newer rates.
Overlaps with Threelines/TAM video lines. Decide which list governs before quoting, or you risk two prices for the same service.
VIP cars, regular cars, shuttle buses.
Treat as provisional until the source is confirmed.
SECTION 2  -  HOW ANY NEW OR ESTIMATED PRICE IS DERIVED

Contracted beats estimated, always. A Threelines or TAM rate is never overwritten by research. Estimates fill gaps only, and every estimated cell is labelled so a reader can tell in one glance which numbers are committed and which are indicative.

Collect the published rate from every supplier that genuinely serves the item. Discard listings that are the same supplier resold under another name - they inflate the sample without adding a real data point.
Take the unweighted mean across suppliers. Unweighted, because the master is a planning rate card, not a forecast of who will actually win the work.

Published rates are usually the cheapest configuration on the cheapest date. Apply a documented uplift to reach what the item actually costs under normal booking conditions, and state the uplift in the cell note. Thin or sole-supplier markets get a smaller uplift, because their headline price already sits close to the real one.
Every estimated figure records: the suppliers sampled, the raw mean, the uplift applied, and the date sampled. An estimate you cannot reconstruct in six months is not usable.

The domestic flight rates follow exactly this method: four carriers sampled per route, codeshare duplicates removed, unweighted mean, then x1.75 where three or more carriers compete and x1.45 on thin routes. Full working is on the Methodology tab of the flights workbook and is the template for anything priced here.
Re-sample estimated lines every six months, and immediately whenever a real quote arrives - at which point the line stops being an estimate and becomes contracted.
SECTION 3  -  HOW TO APPLY THIS TO A LIVE EVENT

Every line in the master scales on exactly one driver. Multiplying a rate by the wrong driver is the single most common way an event budget goes wrong - a per-attendee catering rate treated as fixed will understate a 500-person conference by six figures.
Multiply by headcount. Dominates catering and delegate materials.
Multiply by event days. All crew and staff day rates, vehicles, medical standby.
Charged once regardless of size or duration. Most technical and stage build.
Multiply by number of rooms taken.
Screens and backdrop. Measure the build before costing.
Countable items - barriers, desks, trophies, per speaker, per post.
Fixed-scope output - reports, strategies, videos, packages.
Charged as a % of a stated base, not a SAR amount.
Priced, but the unit is ambiguous or the value looks off. Confirm before use.
No rate on file. Must be quoted before the budget can be closed.
SECTION 3b  -  BUILD SEQUENCE FOR A COSTED EVENT
Lock attendees, event days, rooms, build area (sqm), speaker count and vehicle count before touching a single price. Every downstream number depends on these six figures.
Pick the rows the event actually needs. The master is a catalogue, not a scope - a typical event uses well under half of it.
Line cost = rate x the driver on that row. Never apply a blanket quantity across a mixed category: Catering is per head, Medical is per day, Stage is fixed. They cannot share a multiplier.
Anything flagged REVIEW is priced but its unit is ambiguous. Confirm before it enters a total, or the error scales with the event.
No unpriced line silently becomes zero. Either obtain a quote or record an explicit exclusion, so the total is honest about what it does not cover.
Fees management is a % of a base. Calculate it after the subtotal, and state which subtotal it applies to.
The master holds unit rates, not risk. Contingency is a separate line applied to the subtotal, not baked into individual rates.

1.  Only 3 of 17 companies publish a price. Every big Saudi company (Theeb, Hanco, Lumi, Yelo, Al Faris, Budget) quotes on request only.
2.  Same car, same 8 hours - prices differ by 67%. This is a market where you negotiate.
3.  Only Seyaha says fuel and VAT are included. VAT is 15%, so the cheapest advert is not always the cheapest bill.
4.  Monthly is not always cheaper. A Lexus ES monthly costs 15.5% MORE than booking 26 single days. But luxury cars save 50-60%.
5.  'Limo Riyadh' is a Bahrain company (+973 number), not a Saudi one. Check before you contract.

NOTE: No company was contacted directly - no calls, emails or forms were possible. Every price here is taken from the company's own website (39 prices) or calculated from a published hourly rate (3 prices, marked DERIVED). Nothing is guessed.
